```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo       = TRUE,
  message    = FALSE,
  warning    = FALSE,
  cache      = TRUE,
  cache.lazy = FALSE,   # model objects are large; lazy loading fails on them
  autodep    = TRUE,    # let knitr work out chunk dependencies from object usage
  comment    = "#>",
  fig.align  = "center",
  dpi        = 110
)
options(width = 110, scipen = 6)   # keep counts readable, but let tiny p-values
                                   # stay in scientific notation rather than print as 0

library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(broom)
library(coxme)
library(kableExtra)
library(here)      # portable paths anchored at the repo root (.Rproj / .git)

BASE <- here("data", "processed")   # repo-root/data/processed, wherever the repo lives

# One consistent table style for the whole document.
show_tbl <- function(x, caption = NULL, digits = 3) {
  kbl(x, caption = caption, digits = digits) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                  full_width = FALSE, position = "left", font_size = 13)
}

# HR = exp(coef); returns NA if the term isn't in that model.
hr <- function(fit, term) {
  b <- coef(fit)[term]
  if (is.na(b)) NA_real_ else round(exp(b), 3)
}

# p-values here span 0.97 down to ~1e-11. Rounding to 3 dp would print the tiny
# ones as "0.000", which reads as "exactly zero" - so anything under 0.001 is
# shown in scientific notation instead.
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(is.na(p), NA_character_,
         ifelse(p < 0.001, formatC(p, format = "e", digits = 2),
                           formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))
}
```

# What this document is {.unnumbered}

This is the modelling half of my thesis, run end to end in one place.
Scripts 1-5 build the data; everything from here on fits, diagnoses and
validates the models. I moved it out of the numbered R files and into R
Markdown so that the reasoning, the code and the output sit next to each
other, when I write the thesis I want to be reading my own justification
alongside the number it produced, not flipping between a script and a
console log.

Does an NBA player's recent workload and schedule congestion carry
signal that assist in indicating when a player is at elevated risk of
being injured, and how much of any such signal is real physiology versus
an artefact of who is fit enough to be playing in the first place?

::: {.alert .alert-info}
Every model here is re-fitted from `cox_ready_2021-26.rds` when this
document knits, nothing is read back from a saved model object. Chunks
are cached, so the first knit is slow (the frailty model and the
cross-validation folds dominate).
:::

# The modelling dataset

```{r load-data}
cox <- readRDS(file.path(BASE, "cox_ready_2021-26.rds"))

data_summary <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Player-game intervals (rows)", "Distinct players", "Seasons",
               "New-injury events (primary outcome)",
               "  - soft-tissue", "  - load-linked structural", "  - random-impact",
               "All-injury events (new + reaggravation)",
               "  - soft-tissue", "  - load-linked structural", "  - random-impact"),
  Value = c(
    format(nrow(cox), big.mark = ","),
    format(n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%d (%s to %s)", n_distinct(cox$SEASON), min(cox$SEASON), max(cox$SEASON)),
    format(sum(cox$event), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_soft), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_load), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_impact), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_recurrent), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_soft_recurrent), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_load_recurrent), big.mark = ","),
    format(sum(cox$event_impact_recurrent), big.mark = ",")
  )
)
show_tbl(data_summary, "The counting-process dataset")
```

Each row is one player-game interval `(t_start, t_stop]` with an event
indicator. The clock is **game number within a season**, and a player
only contributes rows while they are genuinely *at risk*, once an injury
starts, the remaining missed games are removed and they re-enter when
they play again. Otherwise I would be counting a player as "surviving"
games they were never available for.

I have 3,257 new-injury events across 1,029 players. Large enough that
**p-values stop being informative on their own**, which is a theme I
return to repeatedly below. At this sample size a trivially small effect
will still return p \< 0.001, so throughout I read effect size first and
significance second.

## What the risk set actually looks like

The at-risk rules are the hardest part of this design to describe in
prose, so here they are drawn. I take LeBron James in 2025-26, because
that one player-season happens to contain every case: a season-opening
absence, a mid-season rest day, a region change during an absence, and
five injury onsets. This reads directly off `panel_2021-26.rds`, before
the risk-set filter in file 5, so the rows that get removed are still
visible.

```{r risk-set-schematic, fig.height=4.6, fig.width=10}
lb <- readRDS(file.path(BASE, "panel_2021-26.rds")) %>%
  filter(PLAYER_NAME == "LeBron James", SEASON == "2025-26") %>%
  arrange(GAME_DATE) %>%
  mutate(
    g      = row_number(),
    tl     = coalesce(INJURY_TIMELOSS, 0L),
    tl_lag = lag(tl, default = 0L),
    onset  = as.integer(coalesce(IS_NEW_INJURY, 0L) == 1 | coalesce(IS_REAGGRAVATION, 0L) == 1),
    pre1st = as.integer(cumsum(coalesce(PLAYED_FLAG, 0L)) == 0),   # left truncation
    # The file-5 rule: out only if already absent when the interval opened AND still absent.
    in_risk = as.integer(!(tl == 1 & tl_lag == 1) & pre1st == 0),
    state = case_when(
      pre1st == 1               ~ "Before first appearance (left-truncated)",
      onset == 1 & in_risk == 1 ~ "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set",
      tl == 1 & in_risk == 0    ~ "Injury absence (removed from risk set)",
      PLAYED_FLAG == 0          ~ "Non-injury absence (at risk, covariates carried forward)",
      tl_lag == 1               ~ "First game back (at risk)",
      TRUE                      ~ "Played (at risk, covariates observed)"))

lev <- c("Played (at risk, covariates observed)",
         "First game back (at risk)",
         "Non-injury absence (at risk, covariates carried forward)",
         "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set",
         "Injury absence (removed from risk set)",
         "Before first appearance (left-truncated)")
pal <- setNames(c("#3d6d99","#7fa8cc","#a8c5dd","#b2182b","#bdbdbd","#efefef"), lev)
lb$state <- factor(lb$state, levels = lev)

TILE <- 0; RISK <- -0.95
ann  <- function(x, y, lab, col = "grey15")
  annotate("text", x = x, y = y, label = lab, size = 2.8, colour = col, lineheight = 0.95)
lead <- function(x, y0, y1)
  annotate("segment", x = x, xend = x, y = y0, yend = y1, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey45")

fig_riskset <- ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = lb, aes(g, TILE, fill = state), colour = "white", linewidth = .3, height = .8) +
  geom_tile(data = lb, aes(g, RISK), height = .34, colour = "grey75", linewidth = .2,
            fill = ifelse(lb$in_risk == 1, "#2f6b3a", "white")) +
  geom_point(data = filter(lb, state == "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set"),
             aes(g, 0.62), shape = 25, size = 2.4, fill = "#b2182b", colour = "#b2182b") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 14, y = 0.95, yend = 0.95, linewidth = .4, colour = "grey45") +
  ann(7.5, 1.62, "Season-opening\nback injury (14 games):\nevent left-truncated") +
  lead(15, 0.45, 2.30) +
  ann(15, 2.55, "Returns at game 15 and\nre-enters the risk set") +
  lead(53, 0.45, 1.05) +
  ann(53, 1.35, "Rested, not injured:\nstays in the risk set") +
  lead(64.5, 0.45, 2.30) +
  ann(64.5, 2.55, "Region changes mid-absence:\nthis onset is lost", "#a0410f") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, seq(10, 80, 10), 82), expand = expansion(add = c(3.5, 1))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(TILE, RISK), labels = c("Scheduled\ngame", "In risk\nset"),
                     limits = c(-1.35, 3.05), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled team game within the season", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.6, colour = "grey25", lineheight = .95),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(9, "pt"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8), legend.margin = margin(t = -2))

fig_riskset
```

Eighty-two scheduled games become **`r sum(lb$in_risk)`** modelled
intervals and
**`r sum(lb$state == "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set")`**
retained events out of the seven onsets in the season. Three things are
worth reading off it.

The **rest day at game 53 stays in the risk set**. That is the case most
easily got wrong: a rested player can still be injured tomorrow, so
dropping them would delete exactly the low-load intervals that identify a
workload effect.

**Game 15 is the first game back**, and it stays in the risk set too.
That one is here because it did not, until I drew this figure. The
original rule was "the previous row was not a time-loss row", which keeps
the onset and removes the absence correctly, but also silently removed
the first appearance *after* every absence. Across the panel that was
4,690 played games, 3.6% of all appearances, and precisely the
return-to-play games `RECENT_RETURN` exists to measure. It cost exposure
rather than events, so no event count was ever wrong, but it removed the
wrong rows. The rule is now
`!(INJURY_TIMELOSS == 1 & INJURY_TIMELOSS_LAGGED == 1)`, which keeps
onsets, keeps returns, and removes only the middle of an absence.

Two onsets are still lost, for different reasons, and both are honest
costs of the design rather than defects. The season-opening back injury
precedes any appearance, so it falls in the left-truncated window. The
onset at game 65 fires while the player is still absent with a different
injury, so the risk-set filter takes it along with the absence around it.
That second case is the one file 5 counts and reports on every run.

# Stage 0 - Covariate screening

Cox models are unstable when two covariates carry nearly the same
information, coefficients effects get split between them, standard
errors inflate, and signs can flip. I have several rolling windows of
the same underlying quantity (7-day, 28-day and 42-day minutes, for
instance). I screen for it *before* fitting, rather than fitting first
and rationalising afterwards.

I use **Spearman** rather than Pearson because these workload
distributions are skewed and I care about monotone redundancy, not
linear redundancy.

```{r stage0-screening}
candidates <- c(
  "ACWR_MIN", "ROLLING_MIN_7D", "ROLLING_MIN_28D", "ROLLING_MIN_42D",
  "SEASON_CUMULATIVE_MIN", "ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "ROLLING_GAMES_28D",
  "ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "ACWR_LOAD",
  "ROLLING_INTENSITY_7D", "ROLLING_INTENSITY_28D", "INTENSITY",
  "ROLLING_DIST_7D", "ROLLING_DIST_28D", "SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
  "TEAM_DAYS_REST", "ROLLING_B2B_7D", "ROLLING_B2B_28D",
  "PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "MIN", "DISTANCE",
  "SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE", "CAREER_GAMES_MISSED", "SEASON_GAMES_MISSED",
  "PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "PLAYER_AGE_AT_GAME", "HEIGHT_INCHES", "WEIGHT",
  "PCT_THROUGH_SEASON"
)
candidates <- candidates[candidates %in% names(cox)]

cor_mat <- cor(cox[candidates], use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
high    <- which(abs(cor_mat) > 0.8 & upper.tri(cor_mat), arr.ind = TRUE)

collinear <- tibble(
  Variable_1 = rownames(cor_mat)[high[, 1]],
  Variable_2 = colnames(cor_mat)[high[, 2]],
  Spearman_r = round(cor_mat[high], 3)
) %>% arrange(desc(abs(Spearman_r)))

show_tbl(collinear, "Collinear pairs (|Spearman r| > 0.8) - only one of each enters the model")
```

## What it shows

23 pairs breach the 0.8 threshold, and they cluster into a few obvious
families: the overlapping minutes windows, the career-length variables,
and the in-game effort measures. For each I keep **one** on
interpretability grounds rather than statistical ones:

-   `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE` (with a quadratic term) over age and draft year:
    tenure is the construct that carries the *institutional* differences
    in how players are worked, and those differences are not linear.
    Under the NBA's **Player Participation Policy (2023)**, teams can
    obtain pre-approved back-to-back rest for players who are 35 or older
    on opening night, or who have accumulated roughly 34,000 regular-season
    minutes or 1,000 career games, or who carry a serious injury history.
    Younger players get no such allowance. So veterans are, by rule as
    well as by convention, rested more and practise less (their acute loads are systematically
    lower), while the same veterans carry the
    most accumulated mileage. Those two forces pull in opposite
    directions across a career, which is exactly the shape a quadratic
    captures and a straight line cannot. The empirical literature agrees
    that the relationship is not a simple line: early NBA epidemiology
    found no clean linear age-injury association (Drakos et al. 2010),
    while more recent work finds older players suffer disproportionately
    under schedule compression (Morikawa et al. 2022), and rookie-season
    injury predicts career longevity at the other end (Martin et al.
    2021). I therefore fit tenure and tenure-squared rather than assume
    monotonicity.
-   `ROLLING_MIN_28D` over the 42-day window: 28 days is the
    conventional chronic window in the ACWR literature, so it keeps my
    results comparable to prior work.
-   `MIN` for in-game effort.

Two specific exclusions worth recording, because both were judgement
calls:

-   **`ROLLING_GAMES_28D` is dropped** (r = 0.86 with chronic minutes).
    It was redundant *and* null when fitted, so nothing is lost.
-   **`ROLLING_GAMES_7D` is kept.** Its correlation with 7-day minutes
    sits under 0.8, and it separates *frequency* from *volume*, playing
    four games in a week is a different stimulus from playing the same
    minutes across two.
