# Stage 1 - Nested models

My hypothesis is ordered, so the model build is ordered too. I add
covariates in three **domain blocks**, workload, then schedule
congestion, then player context, and ask at each, whether the new domain
earns its place. That structure answers "which domain matters", rather
than producing one flat model where I'd be picking through 24
individually significant coefficients.

Three specification choices carry the design, and each is a deliberate
answer to a feature of this data:

| Choice | Why it is there |
|----|----|
| `Surv(t_start, t_stop, event)` | Counting-process form, so covariates can change every game. injured this season y/n model would collapse the season to one outcome and be blind to *when* risk moves. |
| `strata(SEASON)` | Each season gets its own baseline hazard. The COVID-adjacent seasons had a genuinely different shape, and I don't want that contaminating the covariate effects. I assume workload *acts* the same way each season, not that each season is equally dangerous. |
| `cluster(PLAYER_ID)` | LeBron contributes \~332 rows that are one repeatedly-observed person, not 332 independent facts. Without this the standard errors are far too narrow. |

I also **z-score every continuous covariate**, so each hazard ratio
reads as "per 1 standard deviation increase". That is what makes it
legitimate to say chronic load matters more than travel, otherwise I'd
be comparing an effect measured in minutes against one measured in
kilometres.

```{r zscore}
z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))

cox <- cox %>%
  mutate(
    # Workload - minutes & intensity -based
    z_ROLLING_MIN_7D   = z(ROLLING_MIN_7D),
    z_ROLLING_MIN_28D  = z(ROLLING_MIN_28D),
    z_ACWR_MIN         = z(ACWR_MIN),
    z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D = z(ROLLING_GAMES_7D),
    z_MIN              = z(MIN),
    z_PREV_GAME_MIN    = z(PREV_GAME_MIN),   
    z_PREV_2GAME_MIN   = z(PREV_2GAME_MIN), 
    # In-game intensity (distance per minute): LAG versions only, matching the
    # distance/minutes in-game treatment. Rolling and contemporaneous intensity were
    # tested and dropped: both rolling windows were null (7d p=0.92, 28d p=0.16) and
    # the current-game term is not prospective. The lag pair is orthogonal to load
    # (|r| <= 0.06) and jointly significant, so it earns a place as its own construct.
    z_PREV_GAME_INTENSITY    = z(PREV_GAME_INTENSITY),
    z_PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY   = z(PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY),
    # Workload - on-court tracking load (used in Stage 5)
    z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D  = z(ROLLING_LOAD_7D),
    z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D = z(ROLLING_LOAD_28D),
    z_ACWR_LOAD        = z(ACWR_LOAD),
    z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE   = z(PREV_GAME_DISTANCE),
    z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE  = z(PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE),
    # Travel
    z_ROLLING_DIST_7D        = z(ROLLING_DIST_7D),
    z_ROLLING_DIST_28D       = z(ROLLING_DIST_28D),
    z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST = z(SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST),
    # Schedule congestion
    z_IS_B2B = z(IS_B2B),
    z_ROLLING_B2B_7D               = z(ROLLING_B2B_7D),
    z_ROLLING_B2B_28D              = z(ROLLING_B2B_28D),
    z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER = z(PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER),
    z_TEAM_DAYS_REST               = z(TEAM_DAYS_REST),
    # Player context
    z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE     = z(SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE),
    z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED   = z(CAREER_GAMES_MISSED),
    z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON = z(PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON),
    z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON    = z(PCT_THROUGH_SEASON),
    z_HEIGHT_INCHES         = z(HEIGHT_INCHES),
    z_WEIGHT                = z(WEIGHT)
  )
```

```{r model-specs, dependson="zscore"}
surv_lhs <- "Surv(t_start, t_stop, event)"
rhs_tail <- "strata(SEASON) + cluster(PLAYER_ID)"

fit_cox <- function(covariate_terms, lhs = surv_lhs) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0(lhs, " ~ ", paste(covariate_terms, collapse = " + "),
                         " + ", rhs_tail))
  coxph(f, data = cox, ties = "efron")
}

# Workload block - ON-COURT LOAD (tracking distance). I use load rather than minutes
# as my exposure: distance covered is what the body actually absorbed, the sports-
# science "external load", whereas minutes is a coaching decision. Load and minutes
# are ~0.995 collinear here, so this doesn't change discrimination - I verify that
# with a minutes robustness fit below - it just puts the better construct in front.
m1_terms <- c(
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",         # acute on-court load (distance)
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",        # chronic on-court load (distance)
  "z_ACWR_LOAD",               # acute:chronic load ratio
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",        # acute games played (frequency)
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",         # acute travel load
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",        # chronic travel load
  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",  # season-long accumulated travel
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",      # in-game load, last played game (lag-1, load-management signal)
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"      # in-game load, 2 games back (lag-2, prospective fatigue spike)
)

# Intensity (distance per minute) is NOT in the primary model. It is a rate rather than
# a volume, and once volume is controlled it adds nothing. I show that explicitly in the
# intensity robustness fit below, and keep the terms out of Model 3 so the primary model
# doesn't pay intensity's extra missingness (it needs >=10 minutes to be defined).
intensity_terms <- c("z_PREV_GAME_INTENSITY", "z_PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY")

schedule_added <- c(
  "z_IS_B2B","z_ROLLING_B2B_7D", "z_ROLLING_B2B_28D",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST", "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP"
)

context_added <- c(
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE", "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",   # tenure, non-linear: Participation
                                                       # Policy rest allowances vs mileage
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",                             # career durability
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN",          # prior-injury history
  "z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON", "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",           # season timing
  "PLAYED_PRESEASON", "z_HEIGHT_INCHES", "z_WEIGHT"
)

m2_terms <- c(m1_terms, schedule_added)
m3_terms <- c(m2_terms, context_added)

# The minutes-based counterpart of the full Model 3, kept only for the robustness
# check: same specification with minutes swapped in for load - including the same lag-1
# + lag-2 treatment of the in-game term, so the specs differ ONLY in the volume swap.
m3_terms_min <- c("z_ROLLING_MIN_7D", "z_ROLLING_MIN_28D", "z_ACWR_MIN",
                  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D", "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",
                  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST", "z_PREV_GAME_MIN", "z_PREV_2GAME_MIN",
                  schedule_added, context_added)
```

**A note on the in-game load term.** Rather than the current game's
distance, I use two lagged versions: the last game played
(`PREV_GAME_DISTANCE`, lag-1) and two games back (`PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE`,
lag-2). The current game's distance is contemporaneous with the injury
and reverse-caused (a player who breaks down logs a low distance in the
game it happens) so it reads protective for the wrong reason. Both lags
are known before the interval opens, so they are genuinely prospective,
and they separate two signals: the last game carries the load-management
pattern (the game before a breakdown is often a managed, compromised
one, so lag-1 reads protective), while two games back sits before that
compromise and reads as the harmful fatigue spike a real overuse
mechanism should produce.

*I validated that lag-2 survives out-of-sample and is not just
re-expressing the rolling load (VIF ≈ 3) before adopting it. The
trade-off is coverage, a player's first two games each season have no
lag-2 and drop from these models.*

**A note on in-game intensity.** Intensity (distance per minute) is the
*rate* the body worked, as opposed to the *volume* that load and minutes
measure, and it is close to orthogonal to load here (\|r\| ≤ 0.06), so
it is a genuinely separate construct, not a re-labelled one. It is
**not** in the primary model. I tested it and report the result as a
robustness finding below: once volume is accounted for, intensity adds
nothing. Two practical reasons reinforce keeping it out. First, a
per-game rate is only meaningful with a real base of minutes: a
two-minute garbage-time cameo divides distance by a tiny number and
returns a wild rate, so I require at least 10 minutes for an intensity
value, which makes the term *more* missing than the load terms and would
cost the primary model sample for no gain. Second, the rolling windows
(7d and 28d) were flatly null. Intensity is still carried the same
prospective way as everything else (lag-1 and lag-2, no contemporaneous
version) so that the robustness test is a fair one.

A note on the schedule block, I included **both** the accumulated
congestion dose (rolling back-to-back counts, road-trip game number)
**and** the point-in-time flags (`IS_B2B`, `IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP`). The
accumulated versions are the exposure measure. The point-in-time flags
are contaminated by coaching decisions, because a coach rests an at-risk
player tonight. I keep them in so the contrast is visible in the results
table rather than hidden by dropping them, and I mark them as
selection-biased everywhere they appear.

## Model 1 - Workload

```{r m1, dependson="model-specs"}
m1 <- fit_cox(m1_terms)
summary(m1)
```

## Model 2 - Workload + Schedule

```{r m2, dependson="model-specs"}
m2 <- fit_cox(m2_terms)
summary(m2)
```

## Model 3 - Workload + Schedule + Player context

```{r m3, dependson="model-specs"}
m3 <- fit_cox(m3_terms)
summary(m3)
```

## Does each domain earn its place?

The classical likelihood-ratio test does not work here. LRT compares two
log-likelihoods, but `cluster(PLAYER_ID)` doesn't change the likelihood,
it only replaces the variance estimate afterwards. So an LRT would use
the naive likelihood and ignores the correlation corrected for. Instead
I use a **robust Wald test** on the block of newly-added coefficients,
built from the clustered variance-covariance matrix, plus the change in
concordance.

```{r nested-tests, dependson=c("m1","m2","m3")}
# Joint H0 test that the coefficients in a model are all zero, using the
# robust (clustered) covariance. Small p => the block contributes beyond the prior model.
robust_wald <- function(model, added_terms) {
  cf   <- coef(model)
  norm <- function(s) gsub("\\s", "", s)      # I(x^2) spacing varies; match robustly
  idx  <- which(norm(names(cf)) %in% norm(added_terms))
  V    <- vcov(model)[idx, idx, drop = FALSE] # robust vcov of just those coefficients
  b    <- cf[idx]
  stat <- as.numeric(t(b) %*% solve(V) %*% b) # Wald statistic: b' V^-1 b
  tibble(block_df = length(idx), wald_chisq = round(stat, 2),
         p_value  = signif(pchisq(stat, length(idx), lower.tail = FALSE), 4))
}

nested <- bind_rows(
  robust_wald(m2, schedule_added) %>% mutate(block = "Schedule (added to Model 1)"),
  robust_wald(m3, context_added)  %>% mutate(block = "Player context (added to Model 2)")
) %>%
  select(block, block_df, wald_chisq, p_value) %>%
  mutate(p_value = fmt_p(p_value))

concordance_progression <- tibble(
  Model = c("Model 1 - workload", "Model 2 - + schedule", "Model 3 - + player context"),
  Concordance = c(summary(m1)$concordance[1],
                  summary(m2)$concordance[1],
                  summary(m3)$concordance[1]) %>% round(4)
)

show_tbl(nested, "Robust Wald tests on each added block")
show_tbl(concordance_progression, "Discrimination as each domain is added")
```

```{r m3-hr, dependson="m3"}
m3_tidy <- tidy(m3, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(effect_size = abs(estimate - 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(effect_size)) %>%
  select(term, HR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value, robust.se) %>%
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value))

show_tbl(m3_tidy, "Model 3 - hazard ratios, sorted by effect size (not by p)")
```

## Does the exposure choice matter?

I report on-court load, but load and minutes are \~0.995 collinear here,
so a fair question is whether anything hinges on that choice. It does
not. Refitting the *whole* of Model 3 with minutes swapped in for load
leaves discrimination and the headline hazard ratios essentially
unchanged.

```{r robustness-minutes, dependson="model-specs"}
m3_min <- fit_cox(m3_terms_min)   # same Model 3, minutes in place of load

robust_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Concordance", "Chronic workload HR (per SD)",
             "Acute workload HR (per SD)", "ACWR HR (per SD)"),
  `Load (reported)` = c(
    round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), hr(m3, "z_ACWR_LOAD")),
  `Minutes (robustness)` = c(
    round(summary(m3_min)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_28D"), hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_7D"), hr(m3_min, "z_ACWR_MIN"))
)
show_tbl(robust_tab, "Robustness - on-court load vs minutes give the same answer")
```

So the exposure choice is not driving the result. I lead with load
because it is the better *construct*, what the body absorbed rather than
what the coach decided.

## Does intensity add anything beyond volume?

Load and minutes are both **volume** measures. Intensity (distance
covered *per minute*) is the obvious candidate for the thing they miss:
how hard a player worked, not how long. It is nearly uncorrelated with
the load terms here, so if intensity carried independent injury signal
this is where it would show. I add the same prospective lag pair
(previous game, two games back) to the full Model 3 and test whether the
pair is jointly zero.

```{r robustness-intensity, dependson="model-specs"}
# Fit on the rows where intensity is defined for BOTH models, so the comparison is like
# for like (intensity needs >=10 minutes played, so it is missing more often than load).
need_int <- c(setdiff(m3_terms, "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)"), intensity_terms)
cox_int  <- cox %>% filter(if_all(all_of(need_int), ~ !is.na(.)))

m3_int_base <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                     " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_int, ties = "efron")
m3_int_plus <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ",
                     paste(c(m3_terms, intensity_terms), collapse = " + "),
                     " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_int, ties = "efron")

# Joint robust Wald test that both intensity coefficients are zero.
cf <- coef(m3_int_plus); V <- vcov(m3_int_plus); idx <- match(intensity_terms, names(cf))
int_wald <- as.numeric(t(cf[idx]) %*% solve(V[idx, idx]) %*% cf[idx])
int_p    <- pchisq(int_wald, length(idx), lower.tail = FALSE)

intensity_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Concordance", "Chronic load HR (per SD)", "Acute load HR (per SD)",
             "In-game intensity, last game (per SD)", "In-game intensity, 2 games back (per SD)"),
  `Model 3` = c(round(summary(m3_int_base)$concordance[1], 4),
                hr(m3_int_base, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_int_base, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), NA, NA),
  `+ intensity` = c(round(summary(m3_int_plus)$concordance[1], 4),
                hr(m3_int_plus, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_int_plus, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
                hr(m3_int_plus, "z_PREV_GAME_INTENSITY"), hr(m3_int_plus, "z_PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY"))
)
show_tbl(intensity_tab, paste0("Intensity robustness - joint Wald test that both intensity terms are zero: p = ",
                               fmt_p(int_p)))
```

**Intensity adds nothing once volume is accounted for.** Concordance is
unchanged to the third decimal, and the load hazard ratios do not move.
Both intensity hazard ratios are reported **per standard deviation**, the
same scale as every other covariate in this document, and they sit close
to 1. The caveat worth stating plainly: a per-SD move in intensity is a
*small* physical change (these players all move at broadly similar
rates), so this is not evidence that how hard you work is irrelevant, it is
evidence that the *narrow band of intensity visible in public tracking
data* carries no injury signal beyond volume. The high-speed,
high-acceleration component that sports science implicates in soft-tissue
injury is not resolvable in a per-game distance-per-minute average. On
that basis intensity stays out of the primary model.

## Does the deep bench dilute the result?

The sample is every player who appeared at all, and that includes players
at the very end of the rotation: 1-to-20-game seasons, single-digit
minutes. Their availability is driven by coaching and roster politics
far more than by health, so in principle they add at-risk time that is
noise with respect to injury. They are a real share of the rows
(1-to-20-game seasons are about 23% of player-seasons and 11% of rows)
but a much smaller share of the events (under 5%), which is the profile
of observations that dilute rather than inform.

The obvious fix (dropping players with few games *this* season) is a
trap. A player appears in few games precisely *because* he got hurt, so
filtering on this-season availability preferentially deletes the injured
and biases the workload effect toward null. That is conditioning on a
post-baseline outcome. Instead I define the cohort **ex ante**, on the
*previous* season's minutes per game, which is fixed before any of this
season's injuries occur and so cannot be caused by them.

```{r sensitivity-rotation, dependson="model-specs"}
ROTATION_MPG <- 15   # prior-season minutes per game: an established rotation player

# Three groups, not two. PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG is a real 0 for rookies (they genuinely have
# no prior season) but NA for a non-rookie whose prior season is simply absent from the
# record: a season-long injury absence, the G League, or overseas. Those are returning
# players, not deep bench, so file 5 keeps them NA rather than zero-filling them, and
# they are reported separately here instead of being silently pooled with the low-minute
# group. The >= filter drops NA rows, so the cohort is "known rotation player" only.
rot_groups <- cox %>%
  mutate(Group = case_when(
    is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG)              ~ "No prior-season record",
    PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG >= ROTATION_MPG     ~ paste0("Rotation (>= ", ROTATION_MPG, " mpg)"),
    TRUE                                    ~ paste0("Below threshold (< ", ROTATION_MPG, " mpg)"))) %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(`Intervals` = n(), Events = sum(event),
            `Events per 1,000 intervals` = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 2), .groups = "drop")
show_tbl(rot_groups, "Event rate by prior-season role (the dilution, quantified)")

# Pull the three rates out as plain values so the prose can quote them inline
# (an inline `r ...` cannot contain backticks, so no backtick-quoted column names).
rate_of  <- function(pat) rot_groups[["Events per 1,000 intervals"]][grepl(pat, rot_groups$Group)]
rate_low <- rate_of("Below"); rate_rot <- rate_of("Rotation"); rate_na <- rate_of("No prior")
n_noprior <- cox %>% distinct(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG))) %>% pull(n)

# Filtering on PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG alone would drop every one of the no-prior-season
# players, because NA fails the >= test. That is the wrong cut: all of them have real NBA
# history, and the group is Klay Thompson, Kawhi Leonard, Jamal Murray, John Wall, Zion
# Williamson - players missing a season through injury, i.e. exactly the high-burden
# rotation players this sensitivity analysis is supposed to retain. So I fall back to
# CAREER minutes per game where the prior season is missing. Career totals are built from
# seasons BEFORE the modelled one (file 3), so this is still fixed before any of this
# season's injuries occur and the cohort stays ex ante.
cox <- cox %>%
  mutate(CAREER_MPG     = if_else(CAREER_GAMES > 0, CAREER_MINUTES / CAREER_GAMES, NA_real_),
         ROTATION_BASIS = coalesce(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG, CAREER_MPG))

n_restored <- cox %>% distinct(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG) & ROTATION_BASIS >= ROTATION_MPG, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pull(n)

cox_rot <- cox %>% filter(ROTATION_BASIS >= ROTATION_MPG)
m3_rot  <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                 " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_rot, ties = "efron")

rot_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Player-intervals (n)", "Events", "Concordance",
             "Chronic load HR (per SD)", "Acute load HR (per SD)", "ACWR HR (per SD)",
             "In-game load, last game", "In-game load, 2 games back"),
  `All players (primary)` = c(m3$n, m3$nevent, round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
     hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), hr(m3, "z_ACWR_LOAD"),
     hr(m3, "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE"), hr(m3, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")),
  `Rotation players only` = c(m3_rot$n, m3_rot$nevent, round(summary(m3_rot)$concordance[1], 4),
     hr(m3_rot, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_rot, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), hr(m3_rot, "z_ACWR_LOAD"),
     hr(m3_rot, "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE"), hr(m3_rot, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"))
)
show_tbl(rot_tab, paste0("Sensitivity - restricted to established rotation players (>= ",
                         ROTATION_MPG, " mpg in the prior season, or across their career ",
                         "where the prior season is missing)"))
```

The workload result is not an artefact of the deep bench. Restricting to
established rotation players raises the workload hazard ratios: chronic
load goes from `r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` to
`r hr(m3_rot, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` per SD and the ACWR spike from
`r hr(m3, "z_ACWR_LOAD")` to `r hr(m3_rot, "z_ACWR_LOAD")`, with the
lagged in-game structure keeping its shape (protective lag-1, harmful
lag-2). Discrimination goes the other way, from
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 3)` to
`r round(summary(m3_rot)$concordance[1], 3)`.

Both movements have the same cause and neither is a surprise. The
restricted cohort is deliberately more homogeneous, so the effects are
estimated on a cleaner population while there is less variation left to
rank. I keep the full sample as primary because it describes the league
rather than a subset of it, and report this as the check that the
workload effects are not manufactured by the deep bench.

The dilution is visible directly in the event rates above: intervals
below the threshold run at `r rate_low` events per 1,000 against
`r rate_rot` above it, roughly a two-and-a-half-fold difference in how
often the rows actually inform the model.

**A note on how the cohort is defined, because the obvious version of it
is wrong.** Filtering on prior-season minutes alone silently deletes the
`r n_noprior` player-seasons with no prior-season record, since `NA`
fails a `>=` test. Those are not fringe players. Every one of them has
real NBA history, and the group is Klay Thompson, Kawhi Leonard, Jamal
Murray, John Wall, Zion Williamson: players who missed an entire season
through injury. Dropping them from a sensitivity analysis about rotation
players would remove the highest injury-burden veterans in the league on
a technicality, and would bias this check in exactly the direction that
makes it useless. So where the prior season is missing I fall back to
career minutes per game, which restores `r n_restored` player-seasons to
the cohort. Career totals are built only from seasons before the one
being modelled, so the cohort remains fixed in advance and the collider
problem does not return.

I keep the **full sample as primary** (it is the honest population of
NBA players and the broader claim) and report this as the sensitivity
check that the effects survive, indeed sharpen, among the players a
practitioner would actually be managing.

One limitation remains, and one earlier problem is worth recording
because of how nearly it went unnoticed.

The limitation is rookies. They genuinely have no prior season and no
career history to fall back on, so they sit outside this check by
construction rather than by choice.

The earlier problem was the `r n_noprior` non-rookie player-seasons with
**no prior-season record at all**. An earlier version of this build
zero-filled them, which is indistinguishable from a player who logged
zero minutes, so they were quietly swept out with the deep bench. They
are the opposite of deep bench. Their event rate (`r rate_na` per 1,000)
sits above the below-threshold group, and their career minutes run to a
median of about 17 per game. Separating genuine missingness from a true
zero made the problem visible; the career-minutes fallback is what
actually fixed it. The lesson is that a zero-fill and a missing value are
not the same statement, and the difference here was the entire
returning-from-injury population.

## What it shows

Both blocks earn their place, and concordance climbs at each step to
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 3)`. That means given two
comparable player-intervals, the model ranks the one that actually gets
injured as higher-risk about
`r round(100 * summary(m3)$concordance[1])`% of the time, against 50% by
chance. For a model built entirely from **public box-score and schedule
data**, with no access to GPS, medical screening or training-load data,
I think that is the honest near ceiling rather than a disappointment,
and establishing that ceiling is itself a useful finding for anyone
deciding whether public data is sufficient for this task.

Chronic 28-day load is the headline effect at **HR
`r round(summary(m3)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)` per SD**.

What I want to flag as explicitly *not* a finding is that two
point-in-time flags come out looking protective: the back-to-back flag
and the road-trip flag. Playing the second night of a back-to-back reads
as *safer*, which makes no physiological sense. It is **health-gating**:
a coach sits a player who is carrying something, so the flag partly
records who was judged fit that night rather than what they were exposed
to. Both vary between team-mates on the same date, which is the tell.
This is why the accumulated dose measures are the ones I interpret.

**Team days rest is the opposite case, and worth separating out.** It is
protective (HR `r hr(m3, "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST")`), and here that is exactly
what physiology predicts rather than a puzzle. It is also the one
schedule covariate that *cannot* be health-gated: it comes off the
fixture list and every player on a team shares the same value on a given
date, so no decision about an individual can move it. Its SD is about one
day, so the estimate works out at roughly 13% lower hazard per extra rest
day, against the 15.96% lower injury odds Lewis (2018) reports on
different seasons with a different model. On the one covariate where
selection is ruled out by construction, an independent published estimate
comes back almost exactly. It carries no selection asterisk.

`RECENT_RETURN` belongs in that same group, and it is the clearest case
of all. A player in the fortnight after returning carries HR
`r hr(m3, "RECENT_RETURN")`, i.e. materially *lower* hazard, against a
literature that expects return-to-play to be a high-risk window. Nobody
returns until medical staff clear them, and nobody comes back to a full
load: the first weeks back are minutes-restricted and deliberately
ramped. So the covariate measures who was permitted to play, not whether
returning is safe. It carries the same selection asterisk as rest and the
back-to-back flag, and it is a fourth instance of the same mechanism
rather than a separate puzzle.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 2 - The proportional-hazards assumption

The Cox model assumes each covariate's effect is **constant over time**,
that heavy chronic load is as dangerous in game 70 as in game 10. That
is a strong assumption and it is testable. I use scaled Schoenfeld
residuals (`cox.zph`), which essentially ask whether the covariate
values of the players who actually fail drift systematically as the
season progresses.

This stage is a core of the thesis, a violation here is a finding. It
would mean a risk factor intensifies or fades across a season, a dynamic
that only the time-to-event framing can surface at all. So I went in
genuinely hoping to find one.

I set `transform = "identity"` so the time axis stays raw **game
number**. The default Kaplan-Meier transform would compress the axis in
a way that makes the plotted trend hard to reconcile with any
time-interaction I might fit afterwards.

```{r ph-tests, dependson=c("m1","m2","m3")}
zph1 <- cox.zph(m1, transform = "identity")
zph2 <- cox.zph(m2, transform = "identity")
zph3 <- cox.zph(m3, transform = "identity")

zph3_tab <- as.data.frame(zph3$table) %>%
  rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(flag = if_else(term != "GLOBAL" & p < 0.05, "** VIOLATES", "")) %>%
  arrange(term == "GLOBAL", p)

plot_terms <- zph3_tab %>% filter(term != "GLOBAL") %>% pull(term)  # GLOBAL has no curve to plot

zph3_tab %>%
  mutate(chisq = round(chisq, 2), p = fmt_p(p)) %>%
  show_tbl("Model 3 - proportional-hazards test (scaled Schoenfeld residuals)")
```

`r sum(zph3_tab$flag != "")` individual covariates flagged at p \< 0.05
(the two lag in-game load terms among them, at p ≈ 0.002 and 0.007).

## The plots, which is where the decision actually got made

The p-value only tells me a slope isn't exactly zero, at
`r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` events, a near-flat line will
still test significant. The *shape* is what matters, so I plot every
term. A flat line means the assumption holds; a sloping line means the
effect drifts.

```{r schoenfeld-plots, dependson="ph-tests", fig.height=4.2, fig.width=7.5, results="hold"}
for (v in plot_terms) {
  idx <- which(rownames(zph3$table) == v)
  plot(zph3[idx], resid = FALSE, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
       main = paste0("Schoenfeld: ", v, "  (effect vs game number)"))
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
}
```

## What it shows, and why I remedied nothing

At `r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` events the global test is all
but guaranteed to reject (GLOBAL p =
`r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "GLOBAL"])`), and
`r sum(zph3_tab$flag != "")` individual terms flag. But significance is
not the question at this sample size. Two things settle it: the *shape*
of each drift (the plots above), and whether any of it is a biological
effect a time-varying coefficient could legitimately capture.
Decomposing the violators by the *direction* they drift shows it is not.

```{r ph-decomp, dependson=c("ph-tests","m3")}
# Direction of each violation: does beta(t) weaken TOWARD zero (the effect fading) or
# sharpen AWAY from it? Read from the sign of each Schoenfeld residual's drift vs the
# base coefficient - no refitting needed.
bhat <- coef(m3)
vt   <- zph3_tab %>% filter(flag != "") %>% pull(term)
slope_sign <- sapply(vt, function(v) sign(cov(zph3$x, zph3$y[, match(v, colnames(zph3$y))])))
reading <- tribble(
  ~term,                            ~Reading,
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",          "Durability history - frailty compression",
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",           "Load-management signal - selection",
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",          "Fatigue-spike signal - selection",
  "z_ACWR_LOAD",                    "Load spike - selection",
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",            "Experience - survivor pool",
  "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",       "Experience curvature",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "Availability marker",
  "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP",            "Availability marker - sharpening",
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",             "~zero effect (direction immaterial)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",              "~zero effect (direction immaterial)")
decomp <- tibble(term = vt, `HR (per SD)` = round(exp(bhat[vt]), 2),
                 Drift = ifelse(slope_sign != sign(bhat[vt]), "toward 0", "away")) %>%
  left_join(reading, by = "term") %>% mutate(Term = sub("z_", "", term)) %>%
  select(Term, `HR (per SD)`, Drift, Reading)
n_toward <- sum(decomp$Drift == "toward 0"); n_viol <- nrow(decomp)
show_tbl(decomp, "PH violators by drift direction - all selection or context, none biological")

# The obvious remedy, tested: let acute load's effect differ early vs late in the season.
cut <- median(cox$t_stop)
cox$.period <- factor(ifelse(cox$t_stop <= cut, "early", "late"), levels = c("early", "late"))
f_plain <- as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail))
ss_e <- exp(coef(coxph(f_plain, data = filter(cox, .period == "early"), ties = "efron"))["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])
ss_l <- exp(coef(coxph(f_plain, data = filter(cox, .period == "late"),  ties = "efron"))["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])
m_iso <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ",
          paste(c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D*.period"), collapse = " + "),
          " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox, ties = "efron")
iso_e <- exp(coef(m_iso)["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])
iso_l <- exp(coef(m_iso)["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"] + coef(m_iso)[grep(":\\.period", names(coef(m_iso)))])
cidx <- function(fit, d) { d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = d, type = "lp"))
  concordance(Surv(t_start, t_stop, event) ~ .lp, data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance }
tr <- filter(cox, SEASON != "2025-26"); te <- filter(cox, SEASON == "2025-26")
oos_b <- cidx(coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
          " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")), data = tr, ties = "efron"), te)
oos_s <- cidx(coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ",
          paste(c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D*.period"), collapse = " + "),
          " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")), data = tr, ties = "efron"), te)
```

Three points close the case for reporting the proportional model:

1.  **The drift is selection, not biology.** `r n_toward` of the
    `r n_viol` violators weaken *toward* zero across the season - the
    signature of survivor / frailty compression: as the most
    injury-prone players leave the risk pool, the durability and history
    effects (career games missed, the load-management and spike signals)
    fade. The few that sharpen *away* from zero are availability markers
    (the road-trip flag tightening as load-management intensifies late in
    the year), and two of them sit on covariates with essentially no
    effect at all (7-day games and travel, HR ≈ 1.0). None of it is a
    physiological risk that genuinely changes with the calendar.
2.  **The covariate that carries the causal claim is stable.** Chronic
    28-day load tests cleanly proportional (p =
    `r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"])`), and
    so does acute load (p =
    `r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])`). Every
    violation sits on a selection-contaminated or context term - exactly
    the ones I already decline to read causally.
3.  **The standard remedy buys nothing, and I fitted it to find out.**
    When a covariate breaks proportionality the usual fix is to stop
    holding its coefficient fixed and let it change with time. I tested
    that on acute load, since that is the term the causal argument rests
    on, splitting the season in half.

    I fitted it two ways, and the gap between them is instructive. Refit
    the *whole model* separately on each half and the drift looks real:
    HR `r round(ss_e, 2)` early against `r round(ss_l, 2)` late. But that
    lets every coefficient move between halves, so the acute-load change
    is soaking up movement from everywhere else. Fit one model across all
    the rows and let *only* acute load interact with season half, and it
    nearly vanishes: `r round(iso_e, 2)` against `r round(iso_l, 2)`.
    Most of the apparent drift was never acute load's.

    What settles it is the held-out season: concordance
    `r round(oos_b, 4)` proportional against `r round(oos_s, 4)` with the
    time-varying term. It changes nothing about how the model transfers.
    Given every violator drifts for reasons of selection rather than
    biology, a time-varying coefficient would fit that selection rather
    than remove it.

The season dynamic is real, but it lives in the **baseline hazard** -
which climbs materially over the year (quantified in Stage 5) - and
`strata(SEASON)` already absorbs it, so it never needed to be in a
coefficient. A proportional model with a stratified baseline is the
honest and more actionable description: a bad chronic load is a bad
chronic load whenever in the season it lands.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 3 - Reporting and calibration

Using Model 3, this stage produces the numbers that go in the results:
how well the model discriminates, whether its risk score correctly
orders risk, and the final hazard-ratio table organised by domain.

I dont produce a classic absolute-risk calibration curve, and that is a
design consequence, with `strata(SEASON)` there are five baseline
hazards rather than one, and each row is a game-interval rather than a
person, so "predicted 30-day risk" is not well defined here. What my
design supports, is relative-hazard calibration: group intervals by risk
score and check that the observed event rate climbs across the groups.

```{r calibration, dependson="m3"}
cstat <- summary(m3)$concordance
c_est <- cstat[1]; c_se <- cstat[2]
c_lo  <- c_est - 1.96 * c_se; c_hi <- c_est + 1.96 * c_se

cox_lp <- cox %>%
  mutate(risk_score = as.numeric(predict(m3, newdata = ., type = "lp"))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(risk_score))

calib <- cox_lp %>%
  mutate(risk_group = ntile(risk_score, 10)) %>%
  group_by(risk_group) %>%
  summarise(
    n_intervals     = n(),
    events          = sum(event),
    event_rate_1k   = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 2),
    mean_risk_score = round(mean(risk_score), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mono <- cor(calib$risk_group, calib$event_rate_1k, method = "spearman")
show_tbl(calib, "Relative-hazard calibration: observed event rate by risk-score decile")
```

```{r calibration-plot, dependson="calibration", fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7}
fig_calib <- ggplot(calib, aes(risk_group, event_rate_1k)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(title = "Observed injury rate rises monotonically with predicted risk",
       subtitle = paste0("Spearman correlation with decile rank = ", round(mono, 3)),
       x = "Risk-score decile (1 = lowest predicted risk)",
       y = "Observed events per 1,000 intervals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

fig_calib
```

```{r hr-table, dependson="m3"}
domain_map <- tribble(
  ~term,                            ~domain,          ~label,
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",              "Workload",       "Acute on-court load (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",             "Workload",       "Chronic on-court load (28d)",
  "z_ACWR_LOAD",                    "Workload",       "Acute:chronic load ratio",
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",             "Workload",       "Acute games played (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",              "Workload",       "Acute travel load (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",             "Workload",       "Chronic travel load (28d)",
  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",       "Workload",       "Season cumulative travel",
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",           "Workload",       "In-game load, last game *",
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",          "Workload",       "In-game load, 2 games back",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_7D",               "Schedule",       "Acute back-to-back dose (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_28D",              "Schedule",       "Chronic back-to-back dose (28d)",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "Schedule",       "Road-trip game number",
  "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST",               "Schedule",       "Team days rest",
  "z_IS_B2B",                       "Schedule",       "Back-to-back (point-in-time) *",
  "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP",            "Schedule",       "On road trip (point-in-time) *",
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",            "Player context", "Experience (seasons)",
  "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",       "Player context", "Experience squared (inverted-U)",
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",          "Player context", "Career games missed (durability)",
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON",        "Player context", "Prior injury episodes this season",
  "RECENT_RETURN",                  "Player context", "Recently returned (<=14d) *",
  "z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON",           "Player context", "Season progress",
  "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",                "Player context", "Post-All-Star phase",
  "PLAYED_PRESEASON",               "Player context", "Played pre-season",
  "z_HEIGHT_INCHES",                "Player context", "Height",
  "z_WEIGHT",                       "Player context", "Weight"
)

hr_tab <- tidy(m3, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  select(term, HR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) %>%
  left_join(domain_map, by = "term") %>%
  mutate(domain  = factor(domain, levels = c("Workload", "Schedule", "Player context")),
         across(c(HR, conf.low, conf.high), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  arrange(domain, desc(abs(log(HR)))) %>%
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value)) %>%
  select(domain, label, HR, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

show_tbl(hr_tab, "Final hazard ratios (Model 3), by domain - * = selection-biased")

write.csv(hr_tab, file.path(BASE, "final_hazard_ratios_model3.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## What it shows

Concordance is `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4)` (95% CI
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1] - 1.96 * summary(m3)$concordance[2], 3)`-`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1] + 1.96 * summary(m3)$concordance[2], 3)`),
and the risk score orders observed hazard almost perfectly across
deciles (Spearman 1). The model reliably sorts high-risk from low-risk
intervals even though it cannot state an absolute probability. For an
operational use case, who should be managed this week, ranking is the
operative quantity anyway.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 4 - Recurrent-events robustness

Model 3 counts only the first new injury of a kind, which throws away
information, players get injured repeatedly, and that repetition is an
aspect the applied literature cares most. Rather than pick one
recurrent-events model and hope, I fit three that make different
assumptions.

-   **Andersen-Gill (AG)** - every event counts, common baseline,
    marginal interpretation. "what raises the hazard of *any* injury
    onset".
-   **PWP gap-time** - stratifies the baseline by event order (1st / 2nd
    / 3rd+) and resets the clock after each event, so risk is "games
    since last injury". "whether a second injury is intrinsically
    different from a first."
-   **Shared frailty** - a per-player random intercept. Its variance θ
    is a direct, single-number measure of unobserved injury-proneness,
    which is the Martin (2021) claim stated as a testable quantity.

```{r ag-model, dependson="model-specs"}
m3_ag <- fit_cox(m3_terms, lhs = "Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent)")

ag_compare <- full_join(
  tidy(m3,    exponentiate = TRUE) %>% select(term, HR_new_injury = estimate),
  tidy(m3_ag, exponentiate = TRUE) %>% select(term, HR_all_injury = estimate),
  by = "term"
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

show_tbl(ag_compare, "Primary (new injury) vs Andersen-Gill (all injury)")
```

```{r pwp, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
# PWP gap-time: within each player-season, ep_order counts which spell this is, and
# the clock restarts at each event so "time" becomes games since the last injury.
pwp <- cox %>%
  arrange(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, t_stop) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID) %>%
  mutate(ep_order = 1L + cumsum(lag(event_recurrent, default = 0L))) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, ep_order) %>%
  mutate(gap_stop  = row_number(),
         gap_start = gap_stop - 1L) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(ep_order_capped = factor(pmin(ep_order, 3L), levels = 1:3,
                                  labels = c("1st", "2nd", "3rd+")))

stopifnot(all(pwp$gap_stop > pwp$gap_start), all(pwp$gap_start >= 0))

# Drop prior-episode covariates: the event-order strata and the reset clock already show "how many prior injuries" and "how long since"
pwp_terms <- setdiff(m3_terms, c("z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN"))

pwp_fit <- coxph(
  as.formula(paste0("Surv(gap_start, gap_stop, event_recurrent) ~ ",
                    paste(pwp_terms, collapse = " + "),
                    " + strata(SEASON, ep_order_capped) + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")),
  data = pwp, ties = "efron"
)

pwp %>%
  group_by(ep_order_capped) %>%
  summarise(rows = n(), events = sum(event_recurrent), .groups = "drop") %>%
  show_tbl("Events by injury-spell stratum")
```

```{r frailty, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
#a random intercept per player.
frail_fit <- coxme(
  as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent) ~ ",
                    paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                    " + strata(SEASON) + (1 | PLAYER_ID)")),
  data = cox, ties = "efron"
)

theta    <- as.numeric(unlist(frail_fit$vcoef))[1]
sd_frail <- sqrt(theta)
frail_fit
```

A theta on its own is uninterpretable: it says how much players differ in
what I could not measure, but not how much of the original difference I
managed to remove. So I refit the same frailty model with the covariate
blocks added one at a time, starting from nothing. All four are fitted on
the **same rows** (the complete cases the full model uses), otherwise the
variances are not comparable.

```{r frailty-nested, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
# Common row set, so theta is comparable across specifications.
need_f <- gsub("I\\(|\\^2\\)", "", unique(m3_terms))
d_f <- cox %>% filter(if_all(all_of(intersect(need_f, names(cox))), ~ !is.na(.)))

theta_of <- function(terms) {
  rhs <- if (length(terms))
    paste(paste(terms, collapse = " + "), "+ strata(SEASON) + (1 | PLAYER_ID)")
  else "strata(SEASON) + (1 | PLAYER_ID)"
  fit <- coxme(as.formula(paste("Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent) ~", rhs)),
               data = d_f, ties = "efron")
  as.numeric(unlist(fit$vcoef))[1]
}

theta_steps <- c(`No covariates (baseline)` = theta_of(character(0)),
                 `+ Workload`               = theta_of(m1_terms),
                 `+ Schedule congestion`    = theta_of(m2_terms),
                 `+ Player context (full)`  = theta_of(m3_terms))

frailty_tab <- tibble(
  Model = names(theta_steps),
  theta = round(theta_steps, 3),
  `SD (log hazard)` = round(sqrt(theta_steps), 3),
  `Hazard, +1 SD of proneness` = round(exp(sqrt(theta_steps)), 2),
  `90th vs 10th percentile` = round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps)), 2)
)
pct_absorbed <- round(100 * (theta_steps[1] - theta_steps[4]) / theta_steps[1])
show_tbl(frailty_tab, paste0("Between-player heterogeneity as covariates are added (",
                             pct_absorbed, "% of the baseline variance absorbed)"))
```

```{r recurrent-compare, dependson=c("ag-model","pwp","frailty")}
headline <- c("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "z_ACWR_LOAD",
              "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED", "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",
              "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST", "z_IS_B2B", "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN")

hr_from <- function(cf, nm) if (nm %in% names(cf)) round(exp(cf[[nm]]), 3) else NA_real_

compare <- tibble(
  term       = headline,
  HR_AG      = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(coef(m3_ag),    .x)),
  HR_PWP     = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(coef(pwp_fit),  .x)),
  HR_frailty = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(fixef(frail_fit), .x))
)

show_tbl(compare, "Cross-model comparison - AG (marginal) vs PWP (spell strata) vs frailty (conditional)")
```

## What it shows

The headline workload effects hold their shape across all three, the
chronic-load result is not an artefact of how I chose to handle
recurrence.

The frailty variance θ **=** `r round(theta, 3)` is the most interesting
number in this section, but only once it is read against the baseline.
With no covariates at all, θ is `r round(theta_steps[1], 3)`, which puts
the 90th percentile of injury-proneness at
`r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps[1])), 1)`x the hazard of
the 10th. With the full covariate set that spread falls to
`r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)`x. **The model absorbs
`r pct_absorbed`% of the between-player variance.**

Player context does most of that work, taking θ from
`r round(theta_steps[3], 3)` to `r round(theta_steps[4], 3)`, more than
workload and schedule combined. That is what should happen: career games
missed, tenure and prior-episode history are *player-level* attributes,
so they are the terms with any purchase on between-player differences.
Workload moves around within a player across a season, so it was never
going to absorb much of it.

Worth putting the residual next to a measured effect rather than leaving
it hanging. One SD of unmeasured proneness multiplies the hazard by
`r round(exp(sd_frail), 2)`. One SD of chronic load multiplies it by
`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`. The largest thing I measure is bigger
than the largest thing I miss. What remains is a genuine
`r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)`x spread that public data
does not reach, and that is the honest limit rather than a failure.

The instructive divergence is `CAREER_GAMES_MISSED`, which moves from
1.11 under AG to 0.967 under frailty (essentially to null). That is not
a contradiction, it is the two models answering different questions. AG
is marginal (across the population, players with more career games
missed are higher risk). Frailty is conditional (holding a player's own
proneness fixed, their career games missed adds nothing). Both are true:
career games missed is largely a *proxy* for the frailty term, so once
frailty is estimated explicitly, the proxy has no work left to do.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 5 - Mechanism, exposure and hazard trajectory

This is the stage that tests my hypothesis hardest, and where I most
expected to be wrong.

The negative control. If workload genuinely *causes* injury, its effect
should depend on injury type: strong for overuse injuries, weaker for
injuries that are essentially random contact events. If instead workload
predicts every injury type equally, including a finger fracture from a
loose ball, then what I am measuring is not fatigue but exposure:
high-load players are on court more, so more things happen to them.

I split into three tiers rather than the obvious two, because my first
attempt was contaminated and I had to redo it. I originally put all
"traumatic" injuries in the control bucket, but ankle sprains were 42%
of that bucket and are plainly load-related, and I had lumped stress
fractures in with acute ones.

1.  **Soft tissue** - hamstring, calf/Achilles, quad, groin. Load
    *should* drive this.
2.  **Load-linked structural** - ACL/PCL, meniscus, ankle sprain, bone
    stress. Load plausibly contributes; a lower-limb stress fracture is
    almost by definition a load injury.
3.  **Random impact** - finger, eye/face, concussion, dislocation. This
    is the **clean control**. Load should have little effect here beyond
    exposure.

I run the split on the **exact Model 3 specification** (one
specification, three outcomes), so the tiers sit on identical footing
and each tier's hazard ratios are directly comparable to the main Model
3 table. (I originally also ran a separate minutes-vs-distance "which
exposure predicts better" test here; that turned out to be the
tracking-data artefact discussed below, so the exposure question is
settled and this stage is purely the mechanism contrast.)

The trajectory. `basehaz()` reads the baseline hazard directly, telling
me when in a season risk elevates for an average player, independent of
any covariate.

```{r mechanism, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
# Mechanism models use the EXACT Model 3 specification (m3_terms): one specification,
# three outcomes, so the tier hazard ratios are directly comparable to Model 3's table
# and to each other. (An earlier version added rolling + contemporaneous intensity here,
# making this a superset of Model 3; intensity is now folded into Model 3 itself as the
# prospective lag pair, so no separate mechanism specification is needed.)

fit_outcome <- function(outcome, terms) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ ",
                          paste(terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail)),
        data = cox, ties = "efron")
}

m_soft   <- fit_outcome("event_soft",   m3_terms)  # overuse
m_load  <- fit_outcome("event_load",   m3_terms)  # load-linked structural
m_impact <- fit_outcome("event_impact", m3_terms)  # random contact = control
m_soft_load <- fit_outcome("event_soft_load_recurrent", m3_terms)  # random contact = control

m_soft_recurrent   <- fit_outcome("event_soft_recurrent",   m3_terms)  # overuse
m_load_recurrent   <- fit_outcome("event_load_recurrent",   m3_terms)  # load-linked structural
m_soft_load_recurrent <- fit_outcome("event_soft_load_recurrent", m3_terms)  # random contact = control
m_impact_recurrent <- fit_outcome("event_impact_recurrent", m3_terms)  # random contact = control

# The whole model across the three tiers, not just the three load terms. The ratio
# column is the point: it asks which covariates actually DISTINGUISH a load-relevant
# injury from a contact injury. Only one of them does.
mech_terms <- tribble(
  ~term,                     ~label,
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",      "Chronic load (28d)",
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",       "Acute load (7d)",
  "z_ACWR_LOAD",             "Load spike (ACWR)",
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",   "In-game load, 2 games back",
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "Prior injury episodes",
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",   "Career games missed",
  "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",         "Post-All-Star phase")

mech_tab <- mech_terms %>%
  mutate(`Soft-tissue`   = map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_soft,   .x)),
         `Load-linked`   = map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_load,   .x)),
         `Random-impact` = map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_impact, .x)),
         `Soft / impact` = round(`Soft-tissue` / `Random-impact`, 2)) %>%
  select(` ` = label, `Soft-tissue`, `Load-linked`, `Random-impact`, `Soft / impact`)

# Bottom row: each model's overall discrimination (Harrell's C), so the HRs and the
# ranking ability sit in one place.
mech_tab <- bind_rows(mech_tab, tibble(
  ` `             = "Concordance (C)",
  `Soft-tissue`   = round(summary(m_soft)$concordance[1],   3),
  `Load-linked`   = round(summary(m_load)$concordance[1],   3),
  `Random-impact` = round(summary(m_impact)$concordance[1], 3),
  `Soft / impact` = NA_real_
), tibble(
  ` `             = "Events",
  `Soft-tissue`   = sum(cox$event_soft),
  `Load-linked`   = sum(cox$event_load),
  `Random-impact` = sum(cox$event_impact),
  `Soft / impact` = NA_real_
))

show_tbl(mech_tab, "Mechanism split - HR per SD (top rows) and model concordance (bottom row)")
```

The bottom row adds each model's discrimination. The three are close,
but **random-impact is the lowest** at
`r round(summary(m_impact)$concordance[1], 3)`, below soft-tissue
(`r round(summary(m_soft)$concordance[1], 3)`) and load-linked
(`r round(summary(m_load)$concordance[1], 3)`). That's the direction the
negative-control logic predicts: the model ranks the load-relevant
injuries better than the random contact ones, because a random-impact
injury, a jammed finger, a poke in the eye, is by definition the least
driven by the workload, schedule and context the model is built from.

```{r trajectory, dependson="mechanism", fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7.5}
traj <- basehaz(m_soft, centered = FALSE) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(cum_haz = hazard, game_number = time) %>%
  group_by(game_number) %>%
  summarise(cum_haz = mean(cum_haz), .groups = "drop") %>%   # average across season strata
  arrange(game_number)

haz_at <- function(g) traj$cum_haz[which.min(abs(traj$game_number - g))]

early_rate <- (haz_at(25) - haz_at(5))  / 20   # per-game hazard, games 5-25
late_rate  <- (haz_at(75) - haz_at(55)) / 20   # per-game hazard, games 55-75

fig_traj <- ggplot(traj, aes(game_number, cum_haz)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Baseline cumulative hazard steepens as the season progresses",
       subtitle = paste0("Per-game hazard is ", sprintf("%.2f", late_rate / early_rate),
                         "x higher in games 55-75 than in games 5-25"),
       x = "Game number within season", y = "Cumulative baseline hazard") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

fig_traj
```

## What it shows

The mechanism split is the most important result in the thesis, and it
revises my hypothesis rather than simply confirming or refuting it. Read
the table from the bottom row up.

**The model ranks load-relevant injury better than contact injury.**
Concordance is `r round(summary(m_soft)$concordance[1], 3)` for soft
tissue and `r round(summary(m_load)$concordance[1], 3)` for load-linked
structural injury, against
`r round(summary(m_impact)$concordance[1], 3)` for the random-impact
control. A model built from workload, schedule and player context sorts
the injuries those things should govern better than the injuries they
should not. That is the ordering the design predicts, and it is the first
thing I want on the record.

**Acute load is the only covariate in the model that tells the tiers
apart.** It runs
`r round(summary(m_soft)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", 1], 2)` for soft
tissue and
`r round(summary(m_load)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", 1], 2)` for
load-linked structural injury, then falls to
`r round(summary(m_impact)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", 1], 2)` for
random impact. Nothing else in the model does that; every other term sits
between 0.87 and 1.06 on the soft-to-impact ratio. Fatigue can tear a
hamstring and cannot jam a finger, and exactly one covariate behaves
accordingly.

**Everything else is measuring exposure, and that is not a
disappointment.** Chronic load returns its *highest* value in the control
tier
(`r round(summary(m_impact)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 2)`),
which is what an exposure measure should do: a random-impact injury is
close to a pure function of court time, since you have to be on the floor
to be landed on. So the tightest load-to-injury relationship belongs
where contact is the mechanism. I spent a while reading that as a failed
negative control before realising it is the control working: it tells me
which of my covariates are exposure measures and which are not.

The honest summary is that the split **decomposes** the workload result
rather than undermining it. There is an exposure component - chronic
load, ACWR, career context, season phase - that raises the hazard of
everything that can happen on a court. And there is a fatigue component -
acute load - that only raises the hazard of what fatigue can cause. No
pooled-outcome study can separate those two, because without a control
tier they are observationally identical. That separation is the
contribution.

Worth noting the ACWR lands on the exposure side
(`r round(summary(m_soft)$conf.int["z_ACWR_LOAD", 1], 2)` /
`r round(summary(m_load)$conf.int["z_ACWR_LOAD", 1], 2)` /
`r round(summary(m_impact)$conf.int["z_ACWR_LOAD", 1], 2)`), which is
awkward for a measure the literature treats as a fatigue-spike proxy.

A caution I want on the record. I originally saw soft-tissue concordance
jump (0.693 → 0.744) when I first compared on-court distance to minutes,
and read it as external load being a *better predictor*. It turned out
to be a **tracking-data artefact**: DNP games carried a fake zero
distance that the carry-forward then leaked into the injury rows (fixed
in file 4). Corrected, load and minutes are **equivalent**, which is
exactly why I can report load as my exposure (it is the better
*construct*, what the body absorbed rather than what the coach chose)
without it changing a single result, and keep minutes as the Stage 1
robustness check. The lesson: distance is the right construct, but its
apparent *advantage* over minutes was a bug, not a finding.

The trajectory is the clean dynamic finding. Per-game baseline hazard is
`r sprintf("%.1f", late_rate / early_rate)` x steeper in games 55–75
than games 5–25.

Note: it is a property of the baseline hazard, not of any covariate
coefficient, which is precisely why Stage 2 found no covariate drifting.
The season gets more dangerous for everyone; it does not change how
workload acts. Those are different claims and only the survival framing
separates them.

## Does the choice of time scale matter?

Everything above runs on one time axis: the player's sequential position
through their team's **scheduled** games. That is a modelling decision,
not a fact about the data, and it is the sort of decision that usually
goes unexamined in a counting-process model. So I tested the alternative.

The competing clock counts a player's **at-risk intervals** instead,
closing the gaps that injury absences leave behind. Under the scheduled
clock, LeBron's first appearance in 2025-26 is game 15, because his team
played 14 games while he was out. Under the at-risk clock it is game 1.
The difference is not cosmetic: it changes which players sit in the same
risk set. The scheduled clock compares players at the same point in the
season; the at-risk clock compares players at the same number of
available games.

I did consider a third version, counting only games actually *played*,
which is the most literal reading of "the player's own 82 games". It is
not usable. Every event is the first *missed* game of an absence, so a
games-played counter does not advance on the event row and all 3,257
events collapse to zero-length intervals. Making it work would mean
dropping rest days from the risk set, and those rows are deliberately
there: they supply the low-load intervals that identify the workload
effect.

```{r clock-robustness, dependson=c("m3","mechanism")}
cox_b <- cox %>% arrange(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, t_stop) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID) %>%
  mutate(b_stop = row_number(), b_start = b_stop - 1L) %>% ungroup()
stopifnot(all(cox_b$b_stop > cox_b$b_start))

fit_b <- function(outcome, terms = m3_terms) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(b_start, b_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ ",
        paste(terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail)),
        data = cox_b, ties = "efron")
}
m3_b     <- fit_b("event")
msoft_b  <- fit_b("event_soft");  mload_b <- fit_b("event_load")
mimp_b   <- fit_b("event_impact")

clock_tab <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Model 3: chronic load (28d)", "Model 3: acute load (7d)",
               "Model 3: acute:chronic ratio", "Model 3: concordance",
               "Soft-tissue: chronic / acute", "Load-linked: chronic / acute",
               "Random-impact: chronic / acute"),
  `Scheduled-game clock` = c(
    hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
    hr(m3, "z_ACWR_LOAD"), round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
    paste(hr(m_soft,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(m_soft,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(m_load,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(m_load,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(m_impact,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),"/", hr(m_impact,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))),
  `At-risk-interval clock` = c(
    hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
    hr(m3_b, "z_ACWR_LOAD"), round(summary(m3_b)$concordance[1], 4),
    paste(hr(msoft_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), "/", hr(msoft_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(mload_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), "/", hr(mload_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(mimp_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(mimp_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))))

# How far apart are the two clocks in the first place?
clock_gap <- cox_b %>% summarise(
  `Rows where the clocks agree` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*mean(t_stop == b_stop)),
  `Mean absolute difference`    = round(mean(abs(t_stop - b_stop)), 2),
  `Largest difference`          = max(abs(t_stop - b_stop)))

show_tbl(clock_tab, "Time-scale robustness: scheduled-game clock vs at-risk-interval clock")
show_tbl(clock_gap, "How far apart the two clocks actually are")
```

## What it shows

**Nothing moves.** Chronic load goes from
`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` to `r hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`,
acute load from `r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` to
`r hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`, and concordance from
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4)` to
`r round(summary(m3_b)$concordance[1], 4)`. The mechanism split is intact:
acute load still collapses to
`r hr(mimp_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` in the random-impact control under
the at-risk clock while holding up in the two load-relevant tiers.

I had expected chronic load to *fall* under the at-risk clock, on the
reasoning that a clock counting available games would absorb some of the
accumulated-exposure signal the covariate is carrying. It does not; if
anything it rises marginally. The second table explains why: the two
clocks agree on
`r clock_gap[["Rows where the clocks agree"]]` of rows and differ by
`r clock_gap[["Mean absolute difference"]]` games on average. Injury
absences are neither frequent nor long enough to reshape the risk sets.

The one covariate that does move is season progress, which is a
redistribution rather than a finding: once the clock stops tracking
calendar position, the covariate measuring calendar position picks up the
slack.

I keep the scheduled-game clock as primary. It is the axis on which the
baseline hazard has a season interpretation, which is what Stage 5's
trajectory result rests on, and it is the axis that puts players
available on the *same night* in the same risk set, which is the
comparison a team actually makes. But the estimates do not depend on that
choice, and that is worth knowing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 6 - Out-of-sample validation

Everything above reports apparent performance, the model scored on the
same data it was fitted to, which is optimistic by construction. A model
with `r length(coef(m3))` covariates has ample opportunity to fit noise.
So I hold data out and score the frozen model on rows it has never seen,
two complementary ways:

-   **Temporal split**: train on 2021-22 … 2024-25, test on 2025-26.
    This is the operational question: trained on past seasons, does it
    work on a future one? It is how a rolling risk tool would actually
    be operationalised.
-   **Player-grouped 5-fold CV**: each fold holds out whole *players*.
    This is the fair test for repeated-measures data. A naive random row
    split would put LeBron's game 5 in training and his game 6 in test,
    and the model would score well by having memorised him rather than
    by having learned anything general.

Two Notes on the training data:

1.  Z-scores are computed on training rows only and then applied to test
    rows. Scaling on the pooled data would leak the test distribution
    into training.
2.  `strata(SEASON)` is dropped here. A stratified model has no baseline
    for a season it never saw, so it could not score 2025-26 at all.
    Discrimination only needs the linear predictor Xβ, which requires no
    baseline, so a common-baseline fit is both sufficient and necessary
    here.

```{r validation-setup, dependson="model-specs"}
zcols <- c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ACWR_MIN","ROLLING_GAMES_7D",
           "ROLLING_DIST_7D","ROLLING_DIST_28D","SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST","MIN",
           "PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN",
           "ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ACWR_LOAD",
           "PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",
           "PREV_GAME_INTENSITY","PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY",
           "ROLLING_B2B_7D","ROLLING_B2B_28D","PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER",
           "TEAM_DAYS_REST","SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE","CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",
           "PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON","PCT_THROUGH_SEASON","HEIGHT_INCHES","WEIGHT")

# primary = the reported load model; minutes = the same spec with minutes swapped in,
# validated out of sample as the robustness check (both on the new-injury outcome).
specs <- list(
  primary = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ACWR_LOAD","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added)),
  minutes = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ACWR_MIN","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added))
)

# Standardise using TRAIN mean/sd only, then apply that same scaling to test.
add_z <- function(train, test, cols) {
  for (cc in cols) {
    m <- mean(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE); s <- sd(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE)
    train[[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (train[[cc]] - m) / s
    test [[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (test [[cc]] - m) / s
  }
  list(train = train, test = test)
}

# No season strata, so the risk score transfers to unseen seasons/players.
fit_spec <- function(data, spec) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", spec$outcome, ") ~ ",
                          paste(spec$terms, collapse = " + "), " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")),
        data = data, ties = "efron")
}

# concordance(Surv ~ x) treats larger x as LONGER survival; a Cox risk score is the
# opposite, so reverse = TRUE flips it back to the conventional C-index.
c_index <- function(fit, data, outcome) {
  d <- data
  d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = data, type = "lp"))
  concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
              data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance
}
```

```{r temporal-validation, dependson="validation-setup"}
test_season <- "2025-26"
tr0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON != test_season)
te0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == test_season)

temporal <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  sc  <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
  fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
  tibble(model      = nm,
         apparent_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$train, sp$outcome), 4),
         temporal_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$test,  sp$outcome), 4))
})

show_tbl(temporal, paste0("Temporal validation - trained pre-", test_season,
                          ", tested on ", test_season))
```

```{r oos-calibration, dependson="temporal-validation"}
sc    <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
fit_p <- fit_spec(sc$train, specs$primary)

calib_oos <- sc$test %>%
  mutate(risk = as.numeric(predict(fit_p, newdata = ., type = "lp"))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(risk)) %>%
  mutate(risk_group = ntile(risk, 5)) %>%      # 5 bands, not 10 - the test season is smaller
  group_by(risk_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), events = sum(event),
            event_rate_1k = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 1), .groups = "drop")

show_tbl(calib_oos, "Out-of-sample calibration in the held-out season (primary model)")
```

```{r player-cv, dependson="validation-setup"}
set.seed(42)
players <- tibble(PLAYER_ID = unique(cox$PLAYER_ID),
                  fold      = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID))))
coxf <- cox %>% left_join(players, by = "PLAYER_ID")

player_cv <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  oos <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(coxf))          # every row gets a score from a model blind to it
  for (k in 1:5) {
    tr  <- coxf %>% filter(fold != k)       # the other four folds' players
    idx <- which(coxf$fold == k)
    sc  <- add_z(tr, coxf[idx, ], zcols)
    fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
    oos[idx] <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = sc$test, type = "lp"))
  }
  d <- coxf; d$.lp <- oos
  tibble(model = nm,
         player_cv_C = round(
           concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", sp$outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
                       data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance, 4))
})

validation_summary <- temporal %>% left_join(player_cv, by = "model")
show_tbl(validation_summary, "Validation summary - apparent vs two out-of-sample estimates")
```

## What it shows

The gap is roughly **0.01 of concordance** on both models and under both
schemes. That is small, it says the model is not overfitted, and that
its apparent performance is close to what it would deliver on genuinely
new data.

Both out-of-sample schemes need to both return similar conclusions,
because they fail in different ways. The temporal split would expose a
model that only worked in the seasons it was trained on; the
player-grouped CV would expose one that had memorised specific players.

The `minutes` robustness spec lands right on top of the primary (load)
model out of sample - the held-out concordances are identical (see the
table). So the exposure choice, load or minutes, makes no difference to
how the model generalises, which is what I'd expect given they are
\~0.99 collinear.

Out-of-sample calibration holds too, observed injury rates in the
held-out season still climb across risk bands built from the frozen
model. The ranking transfers.
