# Stage 7 - Rolling injury-risk profiles (the applied deliverable)

Everything so far is population-level, hazard ratios, discrimination,
validation. But the thesis set out (§1.7, Aim 1) to build something
operational, a *rolling* profile that captures not just *whether* a
player is at risk but *when* and *why*. This stage turns Model 3 into
that tool.

The mechanics are simple. Model 3's linear predictor is a
per-player-per-game **risk score** (higher = higher hazard) - the same
quantity I calibrated in Stage 3. Plotted over a season it becomes a
trajectory. To make the reading *relative* rather than an
uninterpretable log-hazard number, I overlay the **league risk-set
distribution** at each game number: the median and inter-quartile range
of the score across everyone playing their n-th game of the season. A
line above the band means the player is carrying more modelled risk than
a typical player at that point in the season; the shape shows when.

I use **Model 3** (the primary, validated model) on **2025-26** - the
held-out season, so these are genuinely prospective scores - and pick
three exemplars to span the range: LeBron James as the familiar anchor,
one player the model rates well above the league, and one it rates
below. The test is conceptual: does each profile match what we
independently know about that player's durability and availability?

```{r risk-profiles, dependson="m3", fig.height=8.5, fig.width=8}
TEST <- "2025-26"
cox$risk_lp <- as.numeric(predict(m3, newdata = cox, type = "lp"))
season <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == TEST, !is.na(risk_lp))

# League band: median + IQR of the risk score across everyone at each game number.
band <- season %>% group_by(game = t_stop) %>%
  summarise(q1 = quantile(risk_lp, .25), med = median(risk_lp),
            q3 = quantile(risk_lp, .75), .groups = "drop")

# Three exemplars chosen to span the risk range (see text).
# Player-level check FIRST, so the three exemplars illustrate a relationship rather
# than standing in for one. Mean risk score per player against their injury count.
player_lvl <- season %>%
  left_join(band %>% select(t_stop = game, med), by = "t_stop") %>%
  group_by(PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  summarise(intervals = n(), played = sum(PLAYED_FLAG), events = sum(event),
            missed = max(SEASON_GAMES_MISSED),
            mean_lp = mean(risk_lp), pct_above = mean(risk_lp > med), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(intervals >= 40)

rho_missed <- cor(player_lvl$mean_lp, player_lvl$missed, method = "spearman")

quint_tab <- player_lvl %>%
  mutate(q = ntile(mean_lp, 5)) %>%
  group_by(`Risk quintile` = q) %>%
  summarise(Players = n(),
            `Mean games played` = round(mean(played), 1),
            `Total injury events` = sum(events),
            `Injury events per player` = round(mean(events), 2), .groups = "drop")
rho_events <- cor(player_lvl$mean_lp, player_lvl$events, method = "spearman")
show_tbl(quint_tab, paste0("Player-level risk score against injury count, ", TEST,
                           " (Spearman rho = ", round(rho_events, 2), ")"))

# Three exemplars: two the model ranks correctly, one it does not. Chosen on injury
# EVENTS, not games missed - see the note below on why games missed is the wrong target.
picks <- tibble(
  PLAYER_NAME = c("Jalen Johnson", "LeBron James", "Jamal Shead"),
  role = c("High risk, five injury episodes - ranked correctly",
           "Average risk, three injury episodes - the model's miss",
           "Low risk, no injury episodes - ranked correctly"))

ex <- season %>% inner_join(picks, by = "PLAYER_NAME") %>%
  arrange(PLAYER_NAME, t_stop) %>% group_by(PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  mutate(seg = cumsum(c(1, as.integer(diff(t_stop) > 3)))) %>%  # break the line across absence spells
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(facet = factor(paste0(PLAYER_NAME, "\n", role),
                        levels = paste0(picks$PLAYER_NAME, "\n", picks$role)))
band_f <- tidyr::crossing(facet = levels(ex$facet), band) %>%
  mutate(facet = factor(facet, levels = levels(ex$facet)))
events <- ex %>% filter(event == 1)

# Quantitative check: does the profile match availability + injuries?
prof_tab <- season %>% inner_join(picks, by = "PLAYER_NAME") %>%
  left_join(band %>% select(t_stop = game, med), by = "t_stop") %>%
  group_by(Player = PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  summarise(`Games played`  = sum(PLAYED_FLAG),
            `Injury events` = sum(event),
            `Mean risk score` = round(mean(risk_lp), 2),
            `% games above league median` = round(100 * mean(risk_lp > med)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(`Mean risk score`))
get_stat <- function(nm, col) prof_tab[[col]][prof_tab$Player == nm]
show_tbl(prof_tab, paste0("Exemplar risk profiles vs actual availability, ", TEST))

fig_profiles <- ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = band_f, aes(game, ymin = q1, ymax = q3), fill = "grey80", alpha = .6) +
  geom_line(data = band_f, aes(game, med), colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(data = ex, aes(t_stop, risk_lp, group = seg, colour = facet), linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(data = ex, aes(t_stop, risk_lp, colour = facet), size = .9) +
  geom_point(data = events, aes(t_stop, risk_lp), shape = 4, size = 3, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ facet, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#2166ac", "#1a9850"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = paste0("Rolling injury-risk profiles, ", TEST),
       subtitle = "Model 3 risk score by game. Grey = league IQR, dashed = league median, red x = injury onset.",
       x = "Game number within season", y = "Risk score (Model 3 linear predictor)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
fig_profiles
```

## What it shows

The quintile table above is the general claim: player-level mean risk
score orders injury count across the season (Spearman rho =
`r round(rho_events, 2)`), so the three profiles below illustrate a real
relationship rather than standing in for one.

Two of the three line up, and the third is a miss worth showing.
**Jalen Johnson** sits above the league IQR for essentially the whole
season (`r get_stat("Jalen Johnson", "% games above league median")`% of
his games above the median) and records
`r get_stat("Jalen Johnson", "Injury events")` separate injury onsets,
the highest burden in the season. **Jamal Shead** runs along the bottom
of the band, unbroken across
`r get_stat("Jamal Shead", "Games played")` games, and never records an
injury.

**LeBron James** is where the model gets it wrong, and I want that on the
page rather than glossed. He oscillates around the median, an
average-risk read, yet records
`r get_stat("LeBron James", "Injury events")` injury onsets against
Shead's `r get_stat("Jamal Shead", "Injury events")`. The reason is
visible in the covariates. James's load and schedule profile through
2025-26 is unremarkable, so a model built from workload and schedule has
nothing to flag; what makes him fragile at 40 is age and accumulated
career mileage, which the tenure terms only coarsely capture, plus the
soft-tissue history that public data does not resolve.

**A note on what these profiles are scored against.** The natural
instinct is to validate a risk profile against games missed, and that is
the wrong target. Across all `r nrow(player_lvl)` players with 40 or more
modelled intervals in `r TEST`, mean risk score correlates with games
missed at Spearman
`r round(rho_missed, 2)`. The sign is negative: higher-scoring players
miss *fewer* games, because a high score requires high load and high load
requires being available in the first place. Games missed mixes injury with rest, load management and coaching
decisions. Injury onsets are what the model is fitted to, and they are
what these profiles are judged on.

This is what a concordance of
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 2)` *means* at the individual
level. The model orders roughly two comparable intervals in three
correctly, so about one pair in three is ordered wrongly, and a
three-player figure has no right to be immune from that. A risk profile
that flags its own miss is a more honest description of the tool than
one built from three players who all happen to agree with it.

Two honest caveats. First, the score is **relative**: it ranks, it does
not give an absolute probability - the `strata(SEASON)` design means
there is no single baseline hazard to attach one to. Second, and more
telling, even Shead - my *low-risk* exemplar - sits only modestly below
the median. That is the health-selection wall from Stage 5 made visual:
a player cannot post a very low load-based risk score *and* play a full
season, because availability is exactly what drives the load the score
is built from. The genuinely lowest scores in the league belong to
players barely in the rotation. A profile that is both low-risk and
high-availability is about the best a durable player can look, not a
dramatically empty one.

The *why* lives inside the same object. Because the score is a weighted
sum of the covariates, a player's elevation on any given game decomposes
into how much comes from acute load, schedule congestion, or
prior-injury history - the per-player readout a practitioner would
actually act on. Stage 5 is the population-level version of that same
question.

# Article export {.unnumbered}

Everything the journal article uses is written out from here, so the
article can never drift from this report. Figures go to `docs/figures/`
at print resolution, tables to `docs/tables/` as CSV. Re-knitting
regenerates all of them.

```{r article-export, dependson=c("risk-set-schematic","calibration-plot","trajectory","risk-profiles","hr-table","recurrent-compare","mechanism","player-cv","sensitivity-rotation","robustness-intensity","robustness-minutes","ph-decomp","stage0-screening","nested-tests","oos-calibration","ag-model")}
FIG <- here("docs", "figures"); TAB <- here("docs", "tables")
dir.create(FIG, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(TAB, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Print styling: larger base type than the screen version, because these land in a
# Word document at roughly half the on-screen width.
print_theme <- theme(text = element_text(size = 13),
                     plot.title = element_blank(),      # the article caption carries the title
                     plot.subtitle = element_blank())

save_fig <- function(plot, name, w, h) {
  ggsave(file.path(FIG, paste0(name, ".png")), plot + print_theme,
         width = w, height = h, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
  invisible(name)
}

save_fig(fig_riskset,  "figure1_risk_set_schematic", 10.0, 4.6)
save_fig(fig_calib,    "figure2_calibration_decile",  7.0, 4.5)
save_fig(fig_traj,     "figure3_baseline_hazard",     7.5, 4.5)
save_fig(fig_profiles, "figure4_rolling_profiles",    8.0, 8.5)

# Appendix B1: all 25 scaled-Schoenfeld curves on one sheet. cox.zph plots are base
# graphics, so this is drawn straight to a device rather than through ggsave.
png(file.path(FIG, "appendixB1_schoenfeld_panel.png"),
    width = 10, height = 12.5, units = "in", res = 200)
op <- par(mfrow = c(7, 4), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 2.0, 0.8), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.62)
for (v in plot_terms) {
  idx <- which(rownames(zph3$table) == v)
  plot(zph3[idx], resid = FALSE, lwd = 1.6, col = "steelblue",
       main = sub("^z_", "", v), xlab = "Game number", ylab = "beta(t)")
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey55", lty = 2)
}
par(op); invisible(dev.off())

# Tables. Each is written exactly as the article reports it, so the article can be

}

write_tab(data_summary,            "table1_cohort")

# Conclusion

**1. The mechanism split decomposes workload into exposure and fatigue.**
Chronic load, ACWR and the context terms predict every injury tier at
similar strength, which is what an exposure measure does: court time
raises the hazard of everything that can happen out there, and for a
contact injury exposure *is* the causal route. Acute load is the only
covariate that tells the tiers apart. Both components are real, and no
pooled-outcome study can separate them, because without a control tier
they look identical. That separation is the contribution.

**2. The genuine fatigue signal is acute load, and it is smaller.**
Acute 7-day load fades across the injury tiers in the way a causal
mechanism should.

**3. I report on-court load, but it is interchangeable with minutes -
and catching *why* mattered.** I use load because it is the better
construct (what the body absorbed, not what the coach chose), and the
whole model holds identically under a minutes robustness fit
(concordance `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 2)` either way,
chronic HR \~`r round(summary(m3)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)`
either way). An earlier version had load *out-predicting* minutes for
soft-tissue injury (0.693 → 0.744); that was a tracking-data bug, DNP
games leaking a fake zero distance, not a real edge. Distance is the
right idea, but in NBA public data total load ≈ minutes (r ≈ 0.99) and
the injurious high-speed component is unobserved, so the two are
equivalent.

**4. The season's danger is in the baseline, not the coefficients.**
Per-game baseline hazard is `r sprintf("%.1f", late_rate / early_rate)`
x steeper late season, while covariate effects stay proportional
throughout. Heavy chronic load is equally bad in October and April - the
background risk is what rises.

**5. Injury-proneness is real and largely unmeasured.** θ =
`r round(theta, 3)` implies a
`r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)` x spread between the 90th
and 10th percentile of proneness after adjusting for everything I have.
Public data does not capture it.

## Limitations I want stated plainly

-   Health-gating is not fully solved. Point-in-time rest and
    back-to-back covariates read protective because coaches rest at-risk
    players. I mark them rather than interpret them, but I cannot remove
    the bias with observational data.
-   The outcome is an availability signal, not a diagnosis. Injuries
    come from official pre-game injury reports. I observe "listed Out
    with a reason", not a clinician's diagnosis, and reason text is
    inconsistent.
-   Concordance around 0.68 - 0.73 is a ceiling for public data. No GPS,
    no medical screening, no detailed training load. I'd frame this as
    establishing what public data *can* do rather than as a competitive
    predictive model.
-   The lagged in-game load terms cost coverage. Requiring two prior
    played games means a player's first two appearances each season
    cannot be scored, so the primary model fits
    `r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` new-injury events rather than
    the full `r format(sum(cox$event), big.mark = ",")`. Early-season
    injuries are the blind spot this introduces, a fair price for a
    prospective, correctly-signed load term.
-   The sample includes end-of-rotation players whose availability is
    driven by coaching and roster decisions rather than health. I keep
    them because excluding players on *this* season's games played would
    condition on the outcome, and I show in the rotation-player
    sensitivity analysis that the workload effects hold without them, with
    larger hazard ratios and lower discrimination. But their presence does add at-risk time that is
    largely uninformative about injury.
-   Intensity is measured as a per-game distance-per-minute average, which
    cannot resolve the high-speed and high-acceleration efforts that
    sports science implicates in soft-tissue injury. Its null result is
    evidence about *this* measure, not about intensity as a construct.
-   Mechanism tiers involve judgement. I assign categories by regex on
    reason text. The three-tier split is defensible but not the only
    defensible one.
-   Five seasons, one league. Two are COVID-affected. Season strata
    handle the shape differences but cannot manufacture generalisability
    beyond the NBA.

*Compiled for review: verify each entry's details before the final
reference list. Grouped by role, with a note on where each is used.*

**Statistical methodology**

1.  Therneau TM, Grambsch PM. *Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox
    Model.* New York: Springer; 2000. The counting-process Cox
    framework and time-varying covariates (whole pipeline).
2.  Andersen PK, Gill RD. Cox's regression model for counting processes:
    a large sample study. *Annals of Statistics.* 1982;10(4):1100–1120. The Andersen–Gill recurrent-events model (Stage 4).
3.  Prentice RL, Williams BJ, Peterson AV. On the regression analysis of
    multivariate failure time data. *Biometrika.* 1981;68(2):373–379. The PWP gap-time model (Stage 4).
4.  Grambsch PM, Therneau TM. Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics
    based on weighted residuals. *Biometrika.* 1994;81(3):515–526. The
    scaled-Schoenfeld PH test behind `cox.zph` (Stage 2).
5.  Harrell FE Jr, Califf RM, Pryor DB, Lee KL, Rosati RA. Evaluating
    the yield of medical tests. *JAMA.* 1982;247(18):2543–2546. The
    concordance index (Harrell's C), used throughout for discrimination.
6.  Efron B. The efficiency of Cox's likelihood function for censored
    data. *Journal of the American Statistical Association.*
    1977;72(359):557–565. The Efron approximation for tied event times
    (`ties = "efron"`).

**Applied / domain**

7.  Russell JL, McLean BD, Impellizzeri FM, Strack DS, Coutts AJ.
    Measuring physical demands in basketball: an explorative systematic
    review of practices. *Sports Medicine.* 2021;51(1):81–112. Justifies the on-court external-load (tracking-distance) exposure.
    *(A review of load-monitoring methods; it does not support an
    experience/tenure inverted-U, so it is no longer cited for the
    `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²` term.)*
8.  Chan C-C, Yung PS-H, Mok K-M. The relationship between training load
    and injury risk in basketball: a systematic review. *Healthcare.*
    2024;12(18):1829. The training-load–injury evidence base,
    including U-shaped load–risk findings (motivates the load / ACWR
    block).
9.  Martin *[author initials / journal to verify]* et al. Rookie-season
    injury and career longevity in NBA players. 2021. Durability /
    injury-proneness (frailty stage, and the durability side of the
    `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²` term).
10. Hägglund M, Waldén M, Ekstrand J. Previous injury as a risk factor
    for injury in elite football: a prospective study over two
    consecutive seasons. *British Journal of Sports Medicine.*
    2006;40(9):767–772. Prior injury as a risk factor (the
    prior-episode and recent-return covariates).

**Tenure / age: the non-linear `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²` term**

11. National Basketball Association. *Player Participation Policy.*
    Approved by the NBA Board of Governors, September 2023. The
    institutional mechanism: pre-approved back-to-back rest for players
    aged 35+, or with roughly 34,000 career regular-season minutes or
    1,000 career games, or a serious injury history. Younger players
    receive no equivalent allowance, so acute load differs systematically
    by tenure. *(Formalised from 2023-24; the same veteran-rest pattern
    existed informally earlier in the study window. Note the CBA's "Years
    of Service" provisions govern contracts and salary, not rest, so the
    Participation Policy, not the CBA, is the correct citation here.)*
12. Morikawa LH, Tummala SV, Brinkman JC, Buckner Petty SA, Chhabra A.
    Effect of a condensed NBA season on injury risk: an analysis of the
    2020 season and player safety. *Orthopaedic Journal of Sports
    Medicine.* 2022;10(9). Older players showed disproportionately
    larger injury increases under schedule compression.
13. Drakos MC, Domb B, Starkey C, Callahan L, Allen AA. Injury in the
    National Basketball Association: a 17-year overview. *Sports Health.*
    2010;2(4):284–290. Early NBA epidemiology found no clean *linear*
    age-injury association, supporting a non-linear specification.
